title: Revealing high-dimensional entanglement through symmetry
authors: Jayden Webster, Florian Kanitschar, Emanuele Polino, Simon J. U. White, Sven Rogge, Farzad Ghafari, Marcus Huber, Nora Tischler
abstract: Photons encoded in discrete time bins can be routinely prepared in temporal superposition states, enabling high-dimensional entanglement and enhanced quantum communication rates. However, characterizing this high-dimensional entanglement presents significant challenges, namely due to the involved measurement complexity or reliance on restrictive assumptions that compromise the generality of traditional approaches. Here, we develop and experimentally demonstrate a simple linear-optical scheme based on particle-exchange symmetry that allows us to probe high-dimensional entanglement in time-bin-encoded states. Combining Hong-Ou-Mandel interference with suitable transformations, our method not only certifies entanglement but also lower-bounds its dimensionality using only two dichotomic symmetry-based measurements. This bound is obtained through a new rigorous theoretical analysis and can be further improved by weak, physically motivated assumptions. The scheme remains effective at any timescale, even far below the temporal detector resolution used. Our work provides a powerful state-characterization tool and demonstrates that we can prove high-dimensional temporal entanglement on timescales inaccessible to the setup.
summary: The paper presents a novel linear-optical scheme to certify and lower-bound the dimensionality of entanglement in time-bin encoded photon pairs. By leveraging particle-exchange symmetry and performing measurements via Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, they overcome limitations of traditional characterization methods. This technique provides a scalable tool for verifying high-dimensional quantum resources.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a general method to characterize high-dimensional entanglement, particularly in time-bin encoded photonic states, which traditional methods struggle with due to measurement complexity.
main_result: The authors developed a linear-optical scheme using particle-exchange symmetry that certifies high-dimensional entanglement and provides a rigorous lower bound on its dimensionality using only two simple dichotomic measurements.
method: The method combines Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference with unitary transformations ($U_{\pm}$) and formulates the problem as an optimization program, solved via Semidefinite Programming (SDP) relaxation to find a Schmidt number witness.
model_or_system: The system uses photons encoded in discrete time bins, generated via SPDC. The analysis focuses on bipartite states ($ho$) evolving under specific symmetry operations related to particle exchange.
key_observables: HOM coincidence probabilities ($C_{\exp, \pm}^{	ext{HOM}}$), visibility ($V$), and the entanglement dimension lower bound derived from SDP solutions.
important_parameters: The certified entanglement dimensionality ($k$) relative to the modeled dimension ($d$); time-bin separation ($\sim 9.1 	ext{ ps}$); and measurement outcomes for symmetry projections.
main_assumptions: The approach relies on exploiting particle-exchange symmetry; approximations involve truncating evolved states back onto the initial subspace, which makes the bound conservative but robust.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate HOM interference dependence on particle exchange symmetry (bunching/anti-bunching) and show how certified entanglement dimension increases with the inclusion of physical symmetries like time-invariance and diagonal symmetry.
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical framework using SDP to bound entanglement dimensionality based on measured symmetry projections from HOM interference. It then details an experimental realization using linear optics on time-bin encoded photons, comparing results under various assumed symmetries (e.g., no assumptions vs. full physical constraints).
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, experimentally accessible tool for quantifying entanglement in high-dimensional photonic systems without requiring full state tomography, which is crucial for scaling quantum communication protocols.
